definition: Tile roof replacement removes failing clay or concrete tile and worn underlayment to the deck and installs a new underlayment-and-tile system over a load-rated structure. It renews both the waterproofing layer beneath the tile and the tile covering itself. The underlayment, not the tile, is the real service-life limiter and typically fails well before the tile, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and This Old House.

signs: Interior leaks and ceiling stains under intact tile indicate failed underlayment rather than failed tile, because the underlayment fails well before the tile and is the real service-life limiter on a tile roof, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and This Old House.

Slipped, displaced, or sliding tile across the field indicates corroded fasteners and a deteriorated underlayment that no longer holds the tile course, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance, where the structural detail fails rather than the tile itself.

Broken or cracked tile across more than 20 to 25% of clay or 15 to 20% of concrete crosses the contractor-consensus replacement threshold for a tile roof, per industry repair-vs-replace guidance, because tile cannot be patched and takes a matching-profile replacement.

Spalling and surface flaking on concrete tile indicates freeze-thaw damage from Essex County winters, because Newark crosses the 32°F freezing point repeatedly with an average January low near 25.5°F, per NOAA 1991–2020 normals at Newark Liberty (EWR).

Deteriorated valley, headwall, and chimney flashing under tile admits water at the transitions, because flashing seals the roof transitions that roughly 90 to 95% of leaks trace back to, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA.

A spongy or sagging roof deck under the tile indicates moisture-rotted sheathing from years of underlayment leakage, a structural condition that points toward full replacement rather than a tile-by-tile patch, per GAF inspection guidance.

Daylight through the roof deck seen from inside the attic under a tile roof indicates holes in the decking and a failed underlayment, a sign that points toward replacement rather than a patch, per This Old House.

A tile roof past 50 years with its original underlayment reaches the point where the underlayment outlives its service even as the tile holds, because clay tile lasts 75 to 100-plus years and concrete 40 to 75 years while the underlayment fails sooner, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.
selectionCriteria: Verify New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration, the credential the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs requires of every NJ roofing contractor under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, with the 13VH registration number disclosed on the contract and advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 — a registration, not a license, since NJ issues no roofing license.
Confirm at least $500,000 per-occurrence commercial general liability coverage required of a registered NJ HIC under N.J.S.A. 56:8-142, verified by a current certificate of insurance.
Require a written contract for any home improvement over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2, with an itemized written estimate setting scope, labor, materials, and timeline before work begins.

Confirm a documented structural and underlayment assessment that verifies the deck and framing carry the tile dead load and dates the underlayment before quoting, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance condition guidance, because tile is heavy and the structure carries the load while the underlayment sets the service life.

Confirm the contractor plans a complete tear-off to the deck because a clay or concrete tile roof cannot be roofed-over and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires complete removal of the existing tile covering before new roofing.

Ask for local Essex County references and a written workmanship warranty on the labor, separate from the manufacturer material warranty that covers factory defects when the tile is installed to manufacturer specification.

technicalFacts.fact: Clay tile lasts 75 to 100-plus years and concrete tile 40 to 75 years, against the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart listing clay and concrete tile at 100-plus years.
technicalFacts.source: Tile Roofing Industry Alliance; InterNACHI (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: The underlayment is the real service-life limiter on a tile roof, failing well before the tile, so a tile replacement renews the underlayment and flashing while salvaging or matching the tile profile.
technicalFacts.source: Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and This Old House (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A tile roof cannot be roofed-over and takes a full tear-off to the deck, because the NJ Rehabilitation Subcode requires complete removal of an existing clay, cement, or slate tile covering before new roofing.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, NJ Rehabilitation Subcode (per gold and fact pack §6)

technicalFacts.fact: A complete tear-off and replacement of the tile covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance and requires no construction permit, while a structural change to rafters or trusses to carry the tile load triggers a permit; on a commercial building the replacement requires a permit because the exemption covers only repair of up to 25% of total roof area in a 12-month period.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold and fact pack §6)

technicalFacts.fact: A tile roof is heavy, so the deck and framing carry the tile dead load, and a structural assessment verifies the structure before new tile is set; a structural change to carry the tile load triggers a construction permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.
technicalFacts.source: NJ Uniform Construction Code; Tile Roofing Industry Alliance condition guidance (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Newark crosses the 32°F freezing point repeatedly through winter with an average January low near 25.5°F, driving the freeze-thaw spalling and efflorescence that age concrete tile.
technicalFacts.source: NOAA 1991–2020 normals at Newark Liberty (EWR) (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: The IRC ice-barrier provision (R905.1.2) requires a self-adhering ice barrier from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line in ice-prone climates.

Warranty is two parts: a manufacturer material warranty covering factory defects, preserved when the tile is installed to manufacturer specification, plus the contractor's written workmanship warranty on the labor.
technicalFacts.source: Owens Corning warranty guidance; Integrity Home Exteriors verification guidance (per gold)

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced freeze-thaw climate figure: 'NJ's 60+ annual cycles progressively weaken tiles that would last indefinitely in Florida or Arizona.' Also 'last indefinitely' overstates tile life.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the invented '60+ annual cycles' figure. State the sourced climate fact instead: Newark crosses the 32°F freezing point repeatedly with an average January low near 25.5°F, per NOAA 1991–2020 normals at Newark Liberty (EWR), driving the freeze-thaw spalling on concrete tile. State life as 75 to 100-plus years for clay, 40 to 75 for concrete, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced mechanism claim presented as fact: 'Ice dam formation under tile is particularly destructive because the gap between tile and underlayment traps water that freezes and expands, lifting tiles and breaking their interlocking connections.' No source; the gold's real failure mode is underlayment failure beneath sound tile.
defabToKill.fix: Reframe around the sourced failure mode: the underlayment fails well before the tile and is the real service-life limiter, so leaks appear under intact tile, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and This Old House. Slipped or sliding tile indicates corroded fasteners and a deteriorated underlayment, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.

defabToKill.issue: Vague unsourced threshold: 'widespread cracking' and 'almost certainly failed' with no replacement percentage.
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold's sourced threshold: broken or cracked tile across more than 20 to 25% of clay or 15 to 20% of concrete crosses the contractor-consensus replacement threshold, per industry repair-vs-replace guidance, because tile cannot be patched and takes a matching-profile replacement. A tile roof past 50 years with original underlayment reaches the point where the underlayment outlives its service, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.

defabToKill.issue: Invented flat whole-roof totals not in the gold: 'Clay tile replacement on a typical Essex County home runs $18,000-$35,000 installed. Concrete tile is more affordable at $12,000-$22,000.' The gold carries NO clay-vs-concrete whole-job totals — only $10–$20+/sq ft (NHI Contractors) and a $10,000–$25,000 typical NJ new-roof range.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with gold figures: premium tile installs at $10 to $20-plus per square foot in New Jersey, per NHI Contractors, against a typical NJ new-roof range of $10,000 to $25,000, per HomeAdvisor and Modernize NJ cost data; clay carries a higher material cost than concrete, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.

defabToKill.issue: Invented tile weight figures and disposal-by-weight claim: 'Tile roofs weigh 8-12 pounds per square foot compared to 2-3 pounds for shingles. Disposal fees are correspondingly higher at NJ transfer stations that charge by weight.' Neither the per-sf tile weight nor the transfer-station claim is sourced in the gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the unsourced weights. State the gold's sourced cost driver: tear-off cost rises on a tile roof because a tile roof cannot be roofed-over and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires complete removal of the tile covering to the deck. Keep tile-is-heavy qualitatively only (the structure carries the tile dead load, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance) without a fabricated lb/sq-ft number.

defabToKill.issue: Invented dollar figures for structural engineering and reinforcement: 'a structural engineer's assessment ($400-$800)' and 'Framing reinforcement, if needed, adds $2,000-$8,000.' No source in gold or fact pack; also 'lightweight synthetic tiles that weigh 2-4 pounds per square foot' is unsourced.
defabToKill.fix: Delete the invented dollar figures. State qualitatively from gold: structural reinforcement adds cost when the framing requires upgrading to carry the tile dead load, a structural change that triggers a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7. Drop the synthetic-tile weight number (out of scope: this service is clay and concrete tile).

defabToKill.issue: Invented switch-material whole-roof totals and savings: 'architectural shingles ($8,500-$14,000) or standing seam metal ($12,000-$20,000)' and 'The cost savings from switching materials can be substantial: $5,000-$15,000 less than tile-for-tile replacement.' None of these figures are in the gold; the entire material-switching framing is out of scope for a tile-replacement material page.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the switch-material totals and the $5,000–$15,000 savings claim. Keep the cost section on tile: $10–$20+/sq ft (NHI Contractors) against the $10,000–$25,000 typical NJ new-roof range (HomeAdvisor/Modernize), with NJ sitting 10–40% above national figures (HomeGuide/Integrity Home Exteriors) and a new roof recouping ~60–68% at resale (Zillow/Zonda).

defabToKill.issue: Named manufacturer brand roster presented as routine sourcing: 'Standard profiles from manufacturers like Boral, Eagle, and Ludowici are typically available within 2-4 weeks.' Plus invented lead-time figures '6-12 weeks' and '2-4 weeks' with no source.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the brand roster (Boral/Eagle/Ludowici) and the invented lead-time numbers. Reframe the sourcing point around the gold's real fact: a tile replacement salvages sound tile and matches the profile of replacement tile to the existing roof, because tile cannot be patched and takes a matching-profile course, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced 'standard practice' and batten/counter-batten specifics presented as fact: 'A minimum two-layer underlayment with ice-and-water shield at eaves, valleys, and penetrations is standard practice in our region, even when not code-required'; 'Proper counter-batten spacing and weep-hole placement.' Not in gold or fact pack; the gold's only sourced underlayment/ice fact is the IRC R905.1.2 ice barrier.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the sourced code fact: the IRC ice-barrier provision (R905.1.2) requires a self-adhering ice barrier from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line in ice-prone climates, per the International Residential Code, plus a tile-rated underlayment across the deck. Drop the unsourced two-layer 'standard practice' and counter-batten/weep-hole specifics.

defabToKill.issue: Invented installation timeline: 'Installation timeline for a typical Essex County tile replacement runs 5-10 days.' No source.
defabToKill.fix: Delete the invented day-count. Describe the sourced sequence instead: strip the tile and failed underlayment to the deck, repair the sheathing, install an ice barrier and tile-rated underlayment, and re-lay salvaged and matching tile to manufacturer specification — the sequence that resets the service life on the underlayment that limits it.

defabToKill.issue: Invented annual maintenance budget and per-tile pricing: 'Budget $300-$800 annually for tile replacement and maintenance. Individual cracked tiles cost $30-$80 each to replace.' No source in gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Delete the invented maintenance budget and per-tile prices. Keep maintenance qualitative and grounded: the underlayment is the real service-life limiter, so addressing flashing and underlayment issues prevents the leak cycle; a tile roof cannot be patched indefinitely and broken tile across 20–25% of clay or 15–20% of concrete triggers replacement, per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and industry repair-vs-replace guidance.

defabToKill.issue: 'Custom tile profiles may require 6-12 weeks' and 'factory color matching adds time' presented with confident specificity but no source.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the specific week ranges. State only that matching-profile tile is ordered to arrive on the scheduled start date and that sound tile is salvaged for reuse, per the gold process steps; the decision angle should center on the defining trade-off (underlayment-driven replacement + structural load + mandatory tear-off), not invented lead times.

parentDebtToAvoid: Do NOT reproduce the gold's 'NJ HIC Licensed' credentialsHighlight chip — NJ issues no roofing license; use 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor' / 'registered NJ HIC'.
Do NOT frame NQR as 'licensed' anywhere — the credential is NJ HIC registration (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, 13VH number), not a license.

Do NOT introduce manufacturer brand rosters as NQR partnerships or certifications (no Boral/Eagle/Ludowici cert claims, no GAF/Owens Corning/CertainTeed Master Elite / SELECT ShingleMaster / Preferred). Brands appear ONLY as external data/guidance sources (e.g., Owens Corning warranty guidance, GAF inspection guidance).
Do NOT invent NQR volume ('hundreds of tile roofs replaced') — NQR is a registered NJ HIC serving Essex County, no counts.

Keep the manufacturer material warranty (factory defects, preserved when installed to spec) and the contractor written workmanship warranty (labor) as two distinct, honestly-framed parts — never a single 'lifetime' or brand-certified warranty claim.

articleAngles.signs: The defining sign of a tile roof needing replacement is leaking under intact tile — because the underlayment, not the tile, fails first and is the real service-life limiter (per the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance and This Old House). Other answer-first signs: slipped or sliding tile (corroded fasteners / deteriorated underlayment), broken tile across more than 20–25% of clay or 15–20% of concrete, concrete-tile spalling from Essex County freeze-thaw (NOAA EWR normals), failed flashing at the transitions ~90–95% of leaks trace to (NRCA), a spongy deck, attic daylight, and a 50-plus-year roof on its original underlayment.
articleAngles.costGuide: There IS a real whole-job total: the gold substantiates a $10,000 to $25,000 typical NJ new-roof range (HomeAdvisor/Modernize) alongside a per-square-foot figure of $10 to $20-plus for premium tile (NHI Contractors), with clay costing more than concrete in material. NJ ranges sit 10–40% above national figures (HomeGuide/Integrity Home Exteriors), a new roof recoups ~60–68% at resale (Zillow/Zonda), and the mandatory full tear-off (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, no roof-over) plus any structural reinforcement to carry the tile dead load are the cost drivers — NOT the fabricated $18k–$35k clay / $12k–$22k concrete splits or per-tile/weight figures in the dirty article.
articleAngles.decision: The single most important thing a homeowner should understand: on a tile roof the underlayment fails decades before the tile, so 'replacement' usually means renewing the underlayment and flashing while salvaging or matching the long-lived tile — and because clay/concrete tile cannot be roofed-over, N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 mandates a complete tear-off to the deck, while the tile's dead load means the deck and framing must be verified to carry the weight (a structural change to carry that load triggers a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7). The defining decision factor is underlayment-driven replacement under a mandatory tear-off on a load-rated structure, not the tile itself.
